Operating system roles
Which responsibility belongs to the operating system kernel rather than to an application?
Scheduling which process runs on each CPU core and when
Rendering a web page's layout from its HTML and CSS
Validating the fields a user types into an online form
Compressing a document before it is attached to an email
Scheduling CPU time across processes is a core kernel duty, together with memory, device and file-system management. The other tasks are application logic.
m
CPU privilege levels
On x86-64 hardware, in which privilege ring does an ordinary user application normally execute?
Ring 3, the least privileged level
Ring 0, shared with the kernel itself
Ring 1, reserved for device drivers
Ring 2, reserved for system services
Mainstream operating systems use ring 0 for the kernel and ring 3 for user code; rings 1 and 2 are largely unused.
d
Kernel drivers
Why does a faulty third-party kernel driver pose a greater risk than a faulty application?
It runs with kernel privilege, so a fault can crash or compromise the whole system
It runs in user mode, so the kernel cannot terminate it when it misbehaves
It is loaded before the firmware, so Secure Boot cannot check its signature
It shares memory with every application, so it is always the first target
Drivers run in kernel space with full privilege. A crash there stops the whole OS, and a vulnerable driver can give an attacker kernel-level control.
m
Processes and threads
What do the threads of a single process share with each other?
The process's virtual address space and open handles
A separate copy of the process's entire memory each
Nothing at all, since every thread is isolated by the kernel
Only the CPU registers of the thread that created them
Threads are units of execution within one process. They share its address space and resources but each has its own stack and register state.
d
Process creation
On Linux, how is a new program usually started from an existing process?
The parent forks a copy of itself, and the child replaces its image with exec
The kernel creates the program directly from disk without any parent process
The parent sends SIGSTART to PID 1, which launches the requested program
The parent writes the program path into /proc and the scheduler runs it
fork() creates a child copy and execve() loads the new program into it. That is why every process except PID 1 has a parent.
d
Process trees
A triage shows Microsoft Word spawning powershell.exe, which spawns cmd.exe. Why is this parent-child chain notable?
Office applications rarely need to start shells, so the chain suggests malicious macro activity
Word cannot start child processes at all, so this proves the process tree was forged
PowerShell always starts cmd.exe on launch, so the chain is the expected default
Shells started by Word inherit kernel privilege, so the system is already fully compromised
Unusual parentage is a classic detection signal. Word launching shells is common in macro-based attacks, though it still needs investigation rather than assumption.
m
The /proc file system
What does /proc/<pid>/cmdline show on a Linux system?
The command line with which that process was started
The full list of files the process has written to disk
The process's CPU usage history since the last boot
The user's shell history from the session that started it
/proc exposes live kernel data per process; cmdline holds the arguments it was launched with, which is valuable during triage.
m
Signals
What is the practical difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?
SIGTERM can be caught for a clean exit; SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored
SIGTERM stops a process immediately; SIGKILL asks it politely to stop
SIGTERM applies to threads only; SIGKILL applies to whole process trees
SIGTERM pauses a process for later; SIGKILL saves its memory to disk
SIGTERM (15) lets a process clean up. SIGKILL (9) is enforced by the kernel and gives the process no chance to react.
d
Virtual memory
Why can two processes both use the virtual address 0x7ffd0000 without interfering?
Each process has its own page tables mapping that address to different physical memory
The kernel serialises access so that only one process uses the address at a time
Virtual addresses above 0x7ff00000 are reserved and never point to physical memory
Both processes share the same physical page, but the CPU encrypts it per process
Virtual memory gives each process a private address space. The MMU translates addresses through per-process page tables.
d
Memory protections
What does the NX (no-execute) or DEP protection prevent?
Executing code from memory pages marked as data, such as the stack and heap
Reading memory that belongs to another process on the same system
Writing to the kernel's memory from any user-mode process at all
Loading a program at the same base address on every execution
NX/DEP marks data pages non-executable, so injected bytes placed on the stack or heap cannot simply be run. ASLR is the control that randomises addresses.
m
Memory and investigations
Why is memory valuable evidence in an investigation of a running system?
It holds live processes, connections and decrypted data that may never reach the disk
It is the only place where file-system timestamps are permanently recorded
It keeps a complete history of every process run since the system was installed
It is unaffected by reboots, so it survives when the disk is wiped
Memory holds current state, including injected code and keys, which disappears at power-off. It does not keep long-term history.
m
Firmware
Which statement describes UEFI compared with legacy BIOS?
UEFI is modern firmware that supports features such as Secure Boot and large GPT disks
UEFI is an operating system that replaces the Linux kernel on newer servers
UEFI is a bootloader that runs only after the kernel has finished initialising
UEFI is a Windows service that checks drivers after the user has logged on
UEFI replaced the legacy BIOS interface and adds features including Secure Boot, a boot manager and GPT support.
d
Measured boot
How does measured boot differ from Secure Boot?
Measured boot records hashes of boot components in the TPM for later attestation; Secure Boot blocks unsigned components
Measured boot blocks unsigned components; Secure Boot only records their hashes for administrators to review
Measured boot runs after logon; Secure Boot runs before the firmware initialises any of the hardware
Measured boot applies only to Linux; Secure Boot applies only to Windows systems
Secure Boot enforces signatures; measured boot measures each stage into TPM registers so that the boot path can be verified later.
m
Linux boot sequence
Which order matches a typical modern Linux boot?
Firmware, bootloader (such as GRUB), kernel and initramfs, then systemd as PID 1
Kernel, firmware, systemd, then the bootloader loads the user's desktop
systemd, kernel, firmware, then GRUB mounts the root file system
Bootloader, systemd, firmware, then the kernel starts the login manager
Firmware hands to the bootloader, which loads the kernel and initramfs; the kernel then starts init, normally systemd.
d
Windows boot sequence
On Windows, which process is started by the kernel as the first user-mode process?
smss.exe, the Session Manager
explorer.exe, the Windows shell
svchost.exe, the service host
lsass.exe, the security authority
The kernel starts smss.exe, which sets up sessions and starts csrss and wininit/winlogon. Knowing the normal tree helps spot impostor processes.
m
Services
What distinguishes a service (daemon) from an ordinary interactive program?
It runs in the background, usually without a user session, often from boot
It can run only while an administrator is logged on at the console
It always runs with the identity of the user who installed it
It is written in a special language that only the kernel can execute
Services run in the background, are managed by systemd or the SCM, and often start at boot under a dedicated account.
d
Service security
Why is a service running as LocalSystem a higher risk than one running under a dedicated low-privilege account?
Any compromise of the service gives the attacker full control of the machine
LocalSystem services cannot be stopped, so a fault can never be contained
LocalSystem services bypass the firewall, so they are always exposed online
LocalSystem services write no logs, so their activity cannot be audited
LocalSystem has the broadest local privileges. Least privilege means giving each service only the rights it needs, limiting the blast radius.
d
systemd units
A systemd unit file contains ExecStart=/opt/agent/run.sh. Why should an auditor check the permissions on run.sh?
If a low-privilege user can modify it, they can make the service run their code with its privileges
If the script is world-readable, systemd will refuse to start the service at boot
If the script is owned by root, the service will always run as an unprivileged user
If the script has no execute bit, systemd will run it with root privileges instead
A service runs whatever its ExecStart points to. Writable service binaries or scripts are a common local privilege escalation path.
m
Kernel versus user CPU time
Which tool output gives a first view of running processes and their CPU and memory use on Linux?
top or ps aux
chmod or chown
useradd or passwd
mkfs or fsck
top and ps list processes with resource usage. The other commands manage permissions, accounts and file systems.
